prompt: Why does this lesson test other roles with `psql -h localhost -U bruno shop` instead of `SET ROLE bruno` from ana's session?
hint: When is the first door checked?

choices.text: SET ROLE is not allowed on a role with a password
choices.why: A password has nothing to do with SET ROLE; ana switched to bruno freely in lesson 11.

choices.text: Over the socket, SET ROLE ignores grants
choices.why: SET ROLE checks table privileges faithfully wherever the session came from.

choices.text: -h localhost is faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the socket is if anything quicker.

choices.text: CONNECT is checked when a connection opens, and SET ROLE opens none
choices.why: Right. A test of the database door needs a real login.

prompt: `CREATE ROLE bruno LOGIN ___ ROLE reporting` makes bruno a member of reporting as he is created.
hint: A two-letter keyword.

prompt: Order the three doors a role passes on its way to a row of `reports.sales_by_month`.
hint: Outside in.

prompt: reporting has SELECT on `reports.sales_by_month`, and bruno's query on it fails with `permission denied for schema reports`. What is missing?
hint: Read the last word before the name.

choices.text: SELECT on orders, which the view reads
choices.why: The view reads orders with its owner's rights; bruno read it later with no grant on orders.

choices.text: USAGE on reports
choices.why: Right. A name in a schema cannot even be looked up without USAGE on it.

choices.text: CONNECT on shop, which was revoked from PUBLIC
choices.why: Without CONNECT he would not be in a session to see this error; it would have come at login.

choices.text: The view must be recreated after a GRANT
choices.why: Grants take effect at once; one more GRANT on the schema was enough.

prompt: In `\l shop`, the access list shows `=T/ana`. What does the empty part before `=` mean?
hint: Who is everybody?

choices.text: The owner, written short
choices.why: The owner has its own entry, ana=CTc/ana.

choices.text: A role that was dropped
choices.why: The server refuses to drop a role that holds privileges, so an access list never names a vanished one.

choices.text: A grant still waiting for a reload
choices.why: Grants are catalogue rows and need no reload.

choices.text: PUBLIC: every role, including those created tomorrow
choices.why: Right. Here everybody keeps T, temporary tables, and lost c, connect.

prompt: bruno reads `reports.sales_by_month`, a sum over orders, though he has no privilege on orders. Why?
hint: Whose rights does a view's query run with?

choices.text: Aggregates need no privilege
choices.why: `SELECT count(*) FROM customers` was refused to him directly; aggregates are checked like anything else.

choices.text: A view runs its query with the privileges of its owner, ana
choices.why: Right. The view is a door of its own, letting through what its query produces.

choices.text: USAGE on a schema grants SELECT on its tables
choices.why: USAGE only lets names be looked up; orders is in public, where he has USAGE and was still refused.

choices.text: The view was created WITH security_invoker
choices.why: That option does the opposite: it checks the querying role on the tables underneath.

prompt: An audit script must report, for forty roles, whether each one can read `orders`, without knowing their passwords. What should it call?
hint: The server can answer for any role.

choices.text: `has_table_privilege(role, 'orders', 'SELECT')`
choices.why: Right. It follows memberships the way a real session does, which reading the access list by eye does not.

choices.text: Parse the output of `\dp orders` for each role's name
choices.why: A role with the privilege through a group never appears by name in the list.

choices.text: `SET ROLE` to each one and run a SELECT, trapping the errors
choices.why: It works for tables but costs forty queries on a big table, and misses CONNECT entirely.

choices.text: Read pg_authid
choices.why: pg_authid holds attributes and passwords, not grants on tables.

prompt: On a database created by PostgreSQL 16, what may a role that can connect, and has been given nothing, do in the `public` schema?
hint: `=U/pg_database_owner`

choices.text: Create tables, but not functions
choices.why: bruno's CREATE TABLE was refused at the schema.

choices.text: Nothing at all, not even look up names, until somebody grants USAGE to it
choices.why: PUBLIC still has USAGE on public, which is why bruno's refusal on customers came from the table door.

choices.text: Look names up, but create nothing
choices.why: Right. PUBLIC has U and, since 15, no C.

choices.text: Read every table in it
choices.why: USAGE lets names be looked up; reading a table needs a privilege on the table.

prompt: A database was moved from PostgreSQL 13 to 16 with pg_upgrade. `\dn+ public` shows `=UC/postgres`. What should you conclude?
hint: Which databases does the 15 default reach?

choices.text: pg_upgrade failed halfway and the catalogue is corrupt
choices.why: Keeping the old access list is exactly what a successful upgrade does.

choices.text: PUBLIC still holds CREATE on public, and REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC is due
choices.why: Right. The new default applies to databases created by 15 or later, not to upgraded ones.

choices.text: Nothing: version 16 ignores CREATE on public whatever the list says
choices.why: The server obeys the access list it has; the default is only what a new database starts with.

choices.text: The schema now belongs to pg_database_owner
choices.why: The grantor shown is postgres, the old owner; ownership came across unchanged.

prompt: After `REVOKE CONNECT ON DATABASE shop FROM PUBLIC`, bruno still created a temporary table in a session. Why?
hint: Read the letters left beside the empty grantee.

choices.text: Temporary tables bypass privileges
choices.why: Creating one needs TEMPORARY on the database; it is a privilege like the others.

choices.text: Because the temporary table was created in public, where PUBLIC has CREATE
choices.why: Temporary tables live in a schema of their own per session, and PUBLIC has no CREATE on public.

choices.text: PUBLIC kept T on the database
choices.why: Right. Only CONNECT was revoked; TEMPORARY stays until revoked too.

choices.text: reporting was granted TEMPORARY with CONNECT
choices.why: The grant named CONNECT only; TEMPORARY came from PUBLIC.

prompt: Match each object to what PUBLIC is given on it by default in PostgreSQL 16.
hint: A table you create gives nothing.

prompt: reporting has SELECT on four columns of customers, email not among them. What does `SELECT * FROM customers` give bruno?
hint: What does * ask for?

choices.text: The four columns, with email left out
choices.why: The server does not trim a query to fit a grant; it refuses it.

choices.text: An error naming the table
choices.why: Right. permission denied for table customers, which sends people looking for a table grant.

choices.text: All columns, email shown as NULL
choices.why: No column is ever blanked to fit a grant.

choices.text: An error naming the email column
choices.why: The message names the table, not the column, which is what makes it misleading.

prompt: app has `GRANT SELECT ON customers`. Somebody runs `REVOKE SELECT (email) ON customers FROM app`. Can app still read email?
hint: The two kinds of grant are stored apart.

choices.text: No, the column revoke carves email out of the table grant
choices.why: There is no carving: app read customer1@example.com right after the REVOKE.

choices.text: Yes
choices.why: Right. The REVOKE removed a column grant app never had; the table grant still covers email.

choices.text: No, and app loses the other columns too
choices.why: Nothing was removed at all, so nothing was lost.

choices.text: The REVOKE fails with an error
choices.why: It answered REVOKE, as if it had worked, which is the trap.

prompt: app has only `UPDATE (status)` on orders. Which statement succeeds?
hint: Which statements read a column?

choices.text: `UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 1`
choices.why: WHERE id = 1 reads id, which needs SELECT on it; this was refused.

choices.text: `UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id`
choices.why: RETURNING reads id too, so this fails for two reasons.

choices.text: `UPDATE orders SET total_cents = 0`
choices.why: total_cents is not in the grant.

choices.text: `UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped'`
choices.why: Right, and it changed all million rows: the statement with no WHERE reads nothing.

prompt: To hide email from a role that reads all of customers, revoke the table privilege and grant, by name, the ___ you want to keep.
hint: A list of them goes in brackets after SELECT.

prompt: Row-level security is enabled on customers and there is no policy for reporting. What does bruno's `SELECT count(*) FROM customers` return?
hint: No policy, no rows, and no word about it.

choices.why: That is what ana sees, as a superuser; bruno is filtered.

choices.text: 0, with no warning
choices.why: Right. Default deny, in silence.

choices.text: An error saying no policy exists
choices.why: There is no error, which is what makes the fault hard to find.

choices.text: 10000, the Brazilian customers
choices.why: That needed the reporting_brazil policy, created afterwards.

prompt: An application connects as the owner of its tables. Row-level security with good policies is enabled on them. What does the application see?
hint: Three kinds of role skip the policies.

choices.text: Only the rows its policies allow
choices.why: The owner is exempt unless the table is given FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

choices.text: Every row, because owners are not filtered
choices.why: Right, which is one more reason for the owner to be a separate role.

choices.text: Nothing, because owners need BYPASSRLS
choices.why: Owners skip the policies without that attribute.

choices.text: It gets an error until FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set
choices.why: FORCE would make it filtered; without it, it simply sees everything.

prompt: A nightly pg_dump runs as a role that row-level security filters. What is the right fix?
hint: pg_dump refuses rather than save a filtered copy.

choices.text: Disable row-level security every night before the dump
choices.why: That opens every table to every filtered role for the length of the dump.

choices.text: Run pg_dump with the option that accepts filtered rows
choices.why: It would finish, and the backup would be missing rows nobody notices until a restore.

choices.text: Give the backup role BYPASSRLS
choices.why: Right. That attribute exists for exactly this role.

choices.text: Write a policy USING (true) for every table
choices.why: It works and has to be remembered for every new table; the attribute does not.

prompt: Match each part of row-level security to what it does.
hint: One reads, one writes, one switches, one forces.

pairs.right: The condition a row must meet to be seen
The condition a new or changed row must meet
Applies them to the owner too

prompt: Why does the layout make the owner of every table a role that nobody logs in as?
hint: What can a grant not limit?

choices.text: NOLOGIN roles use less memory
choices.why: A role is a catalogue row; its attributes cost nothing at run time.

choices.text: Because an owner does whatever it likes to its tables, and no grant limits it
choices.why: Right. With no login, there is no password to drop a table with.

choices.text: PostgreSQL forbids an owner from logging in
choices.why: ana owned the tables for most of the lesson and logged in all the time.

choices.text: So that reporting inherits from it
choices.why: reporting is not a member of shop_owner and must not be.

prompt: app inserted into orders with no grant on orders_id_seq. What would have changed if `id` were a `serial` column?
hint: Which kind of column checks its sequence?

choices.text: Nothing; sequences carry no privileges
choices.why: Sequences have privileges, USAGE among them; identity columns just do not check them.

choices.text: app would have to own the sequence
choices.why: A grant is enough; ownership would give far more than needed.

choices.text: The insert would need USAGE on the sequence
choices.why: Right. A serial default calls nextval with app's privileges.

choices.text: The insert would work but skip a number
choices.why: Skipped numbers happen with either kind; the question is the refusal.

prompt: In `\dp`, what does `app=arwd/shop_owner` give app on the table?
hint: a is append.

choices.text: Alter, rename, write and drop
choices.why: Altering and dropping belong to the owner and are not letters in an access list.

choices.text: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE
choices.why: Right: append, read, write, delete; granted by the owner.

choices.text: All privileges, because shop_owner granted them
choices.why: The owner's full set is arwdDxt; app lacks truncate, references and trigger.

choices.text: SELECT on four columns
choices.why: Column grants appear in the Column privileges column, not here.

prompt: A new role `ops` is created with LOGIN and a password, and given nothing else. On shop as left by this lesson, where is its first refusal?
hint: What did layout.sql take from PUBLIC?

choices.text: At the schema public, on its first query
choices.why: PUBLIC still has USAGE on public; and ops never gets that far.

choices.text: At the table, on SELECT from orders
choices.why: That would be the third door; the first one is already shut for ops.

choices.text: At login
choices.why: Right. CONNECT on shop was revoked from PUBLIC and granted only to app and reporting.

choices.text: Nowhere, until pg_hba.conf names ops
choices.why: The host line covers all users; the database refuses it by privilege.

prompt: A support analyst must see only customers of her own country and never their e-mail. Which pair of tools does that?
hint: One hides columns, the other rows.

choices.text: A table grant, plus REVOKE SELECT (email)
choices.why: The column revoke does nothing while the table grant exists, and no rows are filtered.

choices.text: BYPASSRLS and a column grant
choices.why: BYPASSRLS removes the row filter instead of applying it.

choices.text: A policy alone, whose USING leaves email out
choices.why: A policy chooses rows, not columns.

choices.text: A column grant without email, plus a row-level security policy on country
choices.why: Right. Policies narrow what a grant shows; they never replace it.

prompt: Order what each of these controls, from the widest to the narrowest.
hint: A database holds schemas, a schema holds tables, a table holds columns and rows.
items: SELECT on some of its columns
A policy choosing some of its rows

prompt: How many rows did `UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped'` change for app, before the rollback?
hint: All of them.
